title: Articles of Note: Week of August 24, 2026
author: Jason Moore
summary: This weekly roundup from the Classical Ed newsletter, curated by Jason Moore, gathers commentary and excerpts from more than twenty pieces spanning classical education, K-12 policy, and adjacent cultural criticism published in the week of August 24, 2026. Anchoring the collection are two James Hankins essays situating Christopher Nolan's blockbuster film Odyssey within the Western Great Books tradition, alongside pieces on the Pearson Integrated Humanities Program, an Aspen Institute Socrates Seminar on AI and personhood, and Ian Rowe's argument that "ancient intelligence" is the real defense against AI-assisted cheating. The roundup also surveys current K-12 policy debates: school-choice research on why parents choose and leave schools, Rick Hess's interview on the limits of instructional-reform "improvement science," the Gen Z literacy gap following students into college, and Daniel Willingham's rule that students should only use AI for tasks they've already mastered by hand. Several entries move outside strict classical-education territory into general cultural and literary criticism (Shakespeare scholarship, a Wall Street Journal piece on climbing and risk-averse Gen Z, reflections on literary fiction), reflecting the newsletter's broader curatorial range for readers interested in classical schooling, the Great Books, and adjacent K-12 policy debates.
points: The two-part James Hankins essay on Christopher Nolan's Odyssey argues the film participates in, rather than critiques, the Western literary tradition, closing on an image of civilizational renewal rather than condemnation.

Ian Rowe (Washington Examiner) argues that as AI tools make cheating 'virtually undetectable,' the only real defense is the cultivation of virtue and judgment, 'ancient intelligence,' rather than more detection software.

Multiple entries address K-12 policy: EdChoice's Alli Aldis on why parents choose or leave a school, Mike McShane on the 'supply side' of school-choice participation, and Rick Hess's interview with Jal Mehta on why instructional-reform 'improvement science' so often fails to stick.
Daniel Willingham's Fordham Institute piece proposes a guiding rule for student AI use: only use AI for tasks a student can already do well without it.

The roundup also reaches into general cultural criticism outside the education beat: Shakespeare scholarship, a Wall Street Journal piece on Gen Z and risk-averse climbing culture, and a personal essay on why literary fiction 'has lost the plot.'
quotes: Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey is still in movie theaters, and has just passed $700 million in box office receipts.
In fact, at the end of the film, Nolan points to a brighter future for the West by having the sun set behind ravaged Ithaca and the Greek-dominated Aegean Sea
Almost everything we believe about rights, dignity, the correct way to treat others, and the idea of a good life presupposes a stable notion of what constitutes a human being.
A new generation of parents has arrived, people who love their children more visibly, more anxiously, and more attentively than perhaps any generation before them.
Why do parents choose a particular school for their children? It sounds like a simple question, but the reality is more complicated.
Markets are not magic and are shaped by external factors that encourage or discourage participation.

Reports from Notre Dame, Pepperdine, Columbia University, and the University of Virginia have shown that Gen Z students are walking evidence of the failure in the education system that leaves them struggling to read and ill prepared to succeed on the college level.
Most educators agree that there should be some guardrails regarding how students use AI in their independent work.
An elite sport climber died Aug. 3 while attempting a new route in the Sierra Nevada mountains.
